books.section: Topic 4.9 The Development of an American Culture, B. European Romanticism and American Culture

stimulus.text: In the early 1800s many Americans loved the novels of the British writer Sir Walter Scott. His Ivanhoe, set in twelfth-century England, was full of castles, knights, and heroic figures. American writers admired Scott's romantic spirit — its feeling, imagination, and love of a colorful past — but they set their own stories in American places: forests, frontiers, and small towns.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.9 B: Americans were captivated by Scott's novels, with classical historical settings (Ivanhoe was set in twelfth-century England) and larger-than-life heroic figures, and American authors then created literature that drew on Scott's romanticism but was distinctly American. Original synthesis, not a quotation.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Romanticism appealed to many Americans in part because it did which of the following?

options.text: Praised the new factories and their daily routines
options.misconception: Factories were new and impressive, so it is easy to think every new movement praised them.

options.text: An escape from routine into nature and an imagined past
Demanded that all American art copy European castles exactly
options.misconception: Scott's castles are the most vivid image here, so it is easy to make them the rule.

options.text: Rejected all interest in the American past
options.misconception: Romanticism came from Europe, so it is easy to think it ignored America entirely.

rationales.A: Romanticism was a reaction against industrial routine, not a hymn to it.
rationales.B: The market revolution ordered work into routines; romanticism offered forests, feeling, and an older world instead.
rationales.C: American romantics kept the spirit and dropped the castles, setting stories in forests and frontiers.
rationales.D: American writers used romantic feeling on American places and the American past, not against them.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what Americans were escaping. The market revolution was turning work into ordered routine.
2. Ask what romanticism offered instead. Nature, feeling, and a past that felt simpler and more authentic.
Background from the books: romanticism reacted to work becoming ordered around routines and to the valuing of wealth.
Remember: to explain why a movement appealed, find the pressure it relieved.
